summary.text:
Gloucestershire publishes three officer addresses, so it is email-ready, and the report itself is unusually well evidenced. Table 1 ties on all four lines in both years, the section 3.10 borrowing table foots in every cell in both directions, and the balance sheet identity closes to £1,000 — CFR £497.899m less £259.458m of borrowing less £135.591m of other long-term liabilities against the £102.849m of internal borrowing they print.

The lead is section 3.8. Seven temporary loans totalling £55m, printed in full with amount, rate and both dates, at 4.15% to 4.70%. Those are the cheapest inter-authority borrowing rates in our file: in the same winter Cornwall paid 8.50% for four days, Harlow 7.75% for a month, Bexley 7.00% for 32 days and Swale 6.25% for thirteen days. Their £5m at 4.15% ran 17 December to 30 January, straight across the calendar year end.

The consequence is in 3.11: the average cost of their debt FELL from 4.61% to 4.43% in a year when the ten-year certainty rate rose from 5.38% to 5.72%, and they say plainly it was the LA to LA market that did it. They were on both sides of that market at once — borrowing at 4.15-4.70% and lending at 4.5-4.7% — and the portfolio returned 4.73% on an average £232.4m against an average borrowing cost of 4.43%. Their adviser's own benchmark puts them at 5.43% against 4.46% for similar authorities, on lower bail-in exposure and longer duration rather than weaker credit.

Also of record: three Dexia LOBOs, none called in a year when 3.9 says the probability of a call rose; and three £5m rolling credit facilities with housing associations earning a non-utilisation fee while undrawn, which we have seen nowhere else. On today's repayment curve 19 of their 28 PWLB loans price below par, for about £16.5m of net discount — a position their own table note already describes correctly.

officer.body:
Hi Gareth,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Audit & Governance on 23 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. Your section 3.10 table foots in every cell in both directions — the borrowing rows, the external debt column, the movement to £395.049m and the reconciliation back to the £497.898m borrowing requirement. Table 1 ties on all four lines in both years. And the balance sheet closes to a thousand pounds: CFR £497.899m less £259.458m of borrowing less £135.591m of other long-term liabilities is £102.850m, against the £102.849m of internal borrowing you print. Our own PWLB file holds 28 loans at £184,227,599 and a weighted 4.5926%, which sits within two basis points of your 4.61% and about £1.4m under your £185.640m — consistent with your note that the table carries accrued interest, so we make no claim of an exact tie on principal.

We wrote because of paragraph 3.8.

Seven temporary loans, £55m in total, at 4.15% to 4.70%, printed with amount, rate and both dates. Those are the cheapest inter-authority borrowing rates we have seen anywhere this year. For the distribution they sit in: across everything we have read, the same market over the same winter had Cornwall paying 8.50% for four days, Harlow 7.75% for a month, Bexley paying Herefordshire 7.00% for 32 days, and Swale paying Maidstone 6.25% for thirteen days. Your £5m at 4.15% ran 17 December to 30 January — straight across the calendar year end, which your own adviser's paragraph at 3.7 names as one of the two points in the year when this market prices wide.

And paragraph 3.11 is the consequence, which is the part we think is genuinely unusual. The average cost of your borrowing portfolio fell from 4.61% to 4.43% in a financial year when the ten-year certainty rate went from 5.38% to 5.72%. Of the councils we have read this year, almost none can say their debt got cheaper. You can, and 3.11 says exactly why.

The other side of it is that you were on both sides of the same market at once — borrowing at 4.15% to 4.70% and lending to other authorities at 4.5% to 4.7% — with the portfolio returning 4.73% on an average balance of £232.4m against that 4.43% average cost. Your adviser's own comparison puts you at 5.43% against 4.46% for similar authorities, and what is notable is what it isn't bought with: bail-in exposure at 60% against a peer 64%, the same A+ band, and average maturity out at 114 days from 52 a year earlier. That is duration, not credit.

We publish the sector-wide picture of that market precisely because no council can see it from its own trades — you see the 4.15% you got, not whether anyone else got 4.00% or 8.50%. The monthly PWLB side sits alongside it: July was thin, £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, and thin PWLB months are exactly when the inter-authority market prices widest. Both are at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Two smaller notes.

Your table note on the PWLB row reasons about discounts correctly — that some loans are in or close to a discount position, but that repaying would mean replacing them at higher rates. On the DMO's curve this afternoon we can put a figure on the first half of that: 19 of your 28 loans price below par, for £16.9m of gross discount against £0.5m of premium on the other nine, so about £16.5m net. The three £15m loans at 4.25%, 4.46% and 4.55% account for £7.1m of it between them. We're not suggesting anything follows — we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Your note already draws the right conclusion; this just sizes the term in it. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

And your 3.9 — three Dexia LOBOs, none called in a year when you note the probability of a call had risen. That matches what we have picked up everywhere else: ten LOBO calls across seven councils in the last few months, and every single one was either refused or the loan repaid. Not one borrower accepted a higher rate. Dexia is the counterparty in six of the LOBO books we hold. If a call does come, the sector-wide pattern is worth having in front of you.

On training, four fit Gloucestershire. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to 3.8 and the deposit side. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator sizes the discount position. Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) goes to the £90m of strategic funds and the override running to 2029. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
